newsitem.title: CHINA: China soymeal defaults seen hard to quantify.
newsitem.headline: China soymeal defaults seen hard to quantify.

text.p: China has defaulted on soybean meal cargoes, but specific numbers are difficult to pinpoint, grain traders in Hong Kong said on Friday.
Fears of defaults have long circulated in Asian markets, where traders expect frustration in doing business with what they call fickle Chinese buyers.
"You really have to be daring," said one trader who had heard of Chinese buyers defaulting on meal cargoes after the prices dropped.
It was not possible to tell just how many contracts had not been executed and how many more were doomed, traders said.
The U.S. market on Thursday discounted talk that China had cancelled 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes of South American soymeal.
"Nobody knows how much was double booked, or defaulted or sold to others," a trader said.
Traders said they found it very difficult to grasp just how much soybean meal China would import in the second half of the year.
China imported 1.24 million tonnes of soybeans and 1.2 million tonnes of soymeal in January to June this year, customs figures show.
The situation for July to December is much more vague, with huge arrivals expected, but uncertainty over the final picture.
"There have definitely been defaults," said one trader. "The thing to watch now is how much soybean meal China will finally import in the second half of the year."
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) August soymeal ended up $3.70 at $249.00 per tonne on Thursday.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture put 1996/97 net soymeal export sales at 98,300 tonnes with 1997/98 exports at 6,900 tonnes.
